body.heading: Rhymes that keep the rope honest
paragraphs: A skipping rhyme does three jobs at once: it sets the rhythm of the rope, it counts your jumps, and it dares you to keep going. “Cinderella, dressed in yella, went upstairs to kiss her fella — how many kisses did she give him?” Then the counting begins: one, two, three... until the skipper trips, and the number becomes the joke's punchline.

Other rhymes are fortune-tellers: names, places and futures chanted one jump at a time, the rope deciding the answer by when it catches your feet. Children have always known that a game which tells your fortune is better than one that merely counts.

body.heading: From one rope to Double Dutch
paragraphs: With two turners and two long ropes swinging in opposite directions, skipping becomes Double Dutch — a game with Dutch roots that became a dazzling competitive sport in New York in the 1970s, with teams, routines and tricks timed to music. The entry looks impossible until someone shows you: you step in on the beat, as if joining a dance already in progress.

Rhymes vary by street and by decade; children rewrite them constantly, swapping in teachers' names, footballers and television characters. A skipping rhyme is a folk song with a playground for an editor.

body.heading: Try it: write your street's rhyme
paragraphs: Take the Cinderella pattern and rebuild it with local heroes: a name, a place, a silly errand, then a counting question. Test it at the rope — a good rhyme must trip off the tongue at jumping speed, or it will not survive the week.
Then teach it to someone younger. You have joined the oldest publishing industry in the world: no printing press, no copyright, just a rope and a rhyme passed hand to hand.

takeaway: A skipping rhyme is a metronome, a scorekeeper and a fortune-teller in verse — and it belongs to whoever is turning the rope.
